seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #7 — uv add Does Not Pin (and What It Really Writes) (2026)
altTitles: uv add, uv remove, uv tree and dependency groups explained
seo.description: Chapter seven of the uv course. Why uv add writes rich>=15.0.0 rather than a pin, reading the +/~/- markers, uv remove taking seven packages away, uv tree showing pygments needed by both rich and pytest, and dev groups versus extras.
seo.breakdown: why uv add writes a lower bound rather than a pin, what the +/~/- markers mean, and how uv tree exposes a shared dependency.

scenes.narration: Everyone thinks uv add pins the version. It does not. Here's what really happens.

I asked for rich, and uv wrote rich greater-than-or-equal-to fifteen point zero point zero. Read the operator carefully. Not equals — greater than or equal to. So that line is a floor rather than a pin. Which raises an obvious question: if pyproject doesn't pin the version, what does?

uvStage.headline: Read the [operator]
uvStage.premise: uv wrote a lower bound derived from what it installed, not an exact version.

steps.label: uv add rich
steps.detail: installed exactly 15.0.0

steps.label: grep -A2 dependencies pyproject.toml
steps.detail: but wrote a floor, not that exact number

steps.label: grep -m1 -A1 rich uv.lock
steps.detail: and the exact number went in here instead

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter adds packages properly, reads every symbol uv prints while doing it, and shows you the graph uv draws of your own project.

data.title: Adding dependencies
data.subtitle: uv, chapter seven · and what uv add really writes

scenes.narration: Start with the command, then the thing it wrote.

uv add does four jobs at once. uv resolves what your request implies, writes the requirement into pyproject dot toml, updates the lockfile, and installs into your environment. One command where the old world needed three separate ones, and no environment to activate beforehand.

uvStage.headline: One command, [four] jobs
uvStage.premise: Resolve, write, lock, install. All four, from one word, with nothing activated.

steps.label: uv add rich
steps.detail: four jobs, one line, no activation

stage.label: uv add rich
stage.sub: and you typed one of those four words

scenes.narration: So why a floor rather than a pin? Because pyproject dot toml describes what your project can live with, and pinning there would stop anyone depending on your package from ever upgrading rich. The exact version gets recorded somewhere else entirely — the lockfile, which is the next chapter.

uvStage.headline: A floor is a [wider] promise
uvStage.premise: pyproject says what you can live with. The exact version is recorded elsewhere.

steps.label: grep rich pyproject.toml uv.lock
steps.detail: the range here, the exact one there

scenes.narration: You can of course write the range yourself, and uv'll respect whatever you ask for. Quote it, though, because those symbols mean something to your shell too. Pin exactly with double equals, cap an upper bound with less-than, or allow only patch releases with the squiggle-equals form.

uvStage.headline: Write the [range] yourself
uvStage.premise: uv respects whatever specifier you hand it. Quote it — the shell reads symbols.

steps.label: uv add "rich==15.0.0"
steps.detail: exactly this version, and no other

steps.label: uv add "rich>=15,<16"
steps.detail: anything in the fifteen series

steps.label: uv add "rich~=15.0"
steps.detail: patch releases only, so 15.0.x

scenes.narration: Now the symbols uv prints while it works, because they carry real information.

Three markers, and each one means something different. A plus sign marks a package that arrived. A squiggle marks one that changed or got rebuilt. A minus marks one that left. Once you can read all three, uv's output stops being noise and starts being a report you can act on.

uvStage.headline: Plus, squiggle, [minus]
uvStage.premise: Three markers in uv output: added, changed or rebuilt, and removed.

steps.label: uv add --dev pytest
steps.detail: four lines, three different meanings

scenes.narration: Watch what happens when a package leaves. I added httpx earlier, and httpx brought six friends along. Removing httpx takes all seven away, because uv knows nothing else in the project was asking for those six. Chapter zero's install, run backwards.

uvStage.headline: Seven in, [seven] out
uvStage.premise: uv removes what nothing else needs. The install from chapter zero, reversed.

steps.label: uv remove httpx
steps.detail: one asked for, six that came with it

scenes.narration: And now the command that draws your project for you.

uv tree prints the whole dependency graph. Your project at the top, everything it asked for underneath, and everything those things asked for underneath that. But look carefully at this particular tree, because there's something in it worth stopping on.

uvStage.headline: uv draws the [graph] for you
uvStage.premise: Your project, what it asked for, and what those things asked for in turn.

steps.label: uv tree
steps.detail: read the last line, then the fifth

scenes.narration: Pygments appears twice. Once because rich needs pygments, and once because pytest needs pygments too. Two packages asking independently, neither knowing about the other. And yet your environment holds exactly one copy, at one version, shared happily between both.

uvStage.headline: pygments appears [twice]
uvStage.premise: Two packages ask for pygments independently. The shelf holds exactly one copy.

steps.label: uv pip list | grep -i pygments
steps.detail: one copy, not two

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: one copy, and both are satisfied

scenes.narration: Which is exactly the collision from chapter zero, except this time the collision worked out. Both packages happened to accept the same version, so a single copy satisfied both askers. When two packages don't agree, uv refuses rather than overwriting — and that refusal deserves a chapter of its own, coming shortly.

uvStage.headline: The same shelf, [no] collision
uvStage.premise: Both askers accept the same version, so nothing has to be evicted at all.

steps.label: uv pip show pygments | head -4
steps.detail: both names, on one required-by line

scenes.narration: Last piece: not every dependency is the same kind of dependency.

Pytest is a test runner. Your code doesn't need pytest in order to run — you're the one who needs pytest, in order to develop. So it goes in a development group instead, and anyone installing your package as a library never receives it.

uvStage.headline: Development is a [group]
uvStage.premise: Tools you need to build the thing are separated from what the thing needs to run.

steps.label: uv add --dev pytest
steps.detail: into a group, not into dependencies

steps.label: grep -A3 dependency-groups pyproject.toml
steps.detail: a separate block, deliberately

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: installing your library never brings pytest

scenes.narration: There're two more shapes worth knowing. Named groups let you separate docs tooling from lint tooling from test tooling. And optional dependencies become extras — things a user of your package opts into by name, rather than receiving whether they want them or not.

uvStage.headline: Groups, and [extras]
uvStage.premise: Groups are for you. Extras are for whoever installs your package later.
uvStage.stageTitle: four places a package can go

steps.label: uv add --group docs mkdocs
steps.detail: a named group, just for you

steps.label: uv add --optional pdf reportlab
steps.detail: an extra, for whoever installs you

stage.label: --group docs
stage.sub: and only when you ask for it

stage.label: --optional pdf
stage.sub: a user asks for it by name

stage.label: pip install you[pdf]
stage.sub: which is how an extra gets requested

scenes.narration: Three more sources are worth knowing about, because not everything you'll depend on lives on PyPI. uv will take a package from a git repository, from a folder on your own disk, or from a plain URL — and each one is written into pyproject so your colleague gets the same source you did.

uvStage.headline: Not everything comes from [PyPI]
uvStage.premise: Git, a local folder, or a URL. Each is recorded, so the source travels too.

steps.label: uv add "httpx @ git+https://github.com/encode/httpx"
steps.detail: an unreleased branch, recorded properly

stage.label: git+https://...
stage.sub: a branch, a tag, or one commit

stage.label: --editable ../lib
stage.sub: a folder on your own disk

stage.label: https://.../x.whl
stage.sub: a file somewhere on the internet

scenes.narration: One flag deserves a mention on its own, because it's about how you work rather than what you install. Editable means uv points at a folder instead of copying it, so a change you make in that folder is live immediately, with nothing to reinstall.

uvStage.headline: Editable points, it does not [copy]
uvStage.premise: The project links to your folder, so an edit there is live without reinstalling.
uvStage.stageTitle: working on two things at once

steps.label: uv add --editable ../shared-utils
steps.detail: a link, not a copy

steps.label: echo "def hi(): return 1" >> ../shared-utils/src/u.py
steps.detail: edit the other project...

steps.label: uv run python -c "import u; print(u.hi())"
steps.detail: ...and no reinstall was needed

stage.label: invoice-app
stage.sub: the project you are working in

scenes.narration: And when you want a newer version of something, uv's upgrade-package flag moves exactly one thing forward and leaves the rest of the lockfile untouched. Which matters, because upgrading everything at once is how a working project becomes a debugging session.

uvStage.headline: Move [one] thing forward
uvStage.premise: Upgrading one package rewrites one line of the lockfile, and nothing else.

steps.label: uv lock --upgrade-package rich
steps.detail: one line changed, twelve untouched

stage.label: pytest
stage.sub: and everything else stayed exactly put

scenes.narration: Quick check. uv add rich wrote rich greater-than-or-equal-to fifteen. Your colleague clones the repo next month, when sixteen is out. Which version do they get? Pause the video here and think it through before I answer. Ready? Fifteen — because the lockfile decides, not that range.

quiz.question: Range says >=15, and 16 is out. What do they get?
quiz.why: The range says what is allowed. The lock says what you get.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. uv add writes a floor rather than a pin, because pyproject describes what your project can live with. Plus, squiggle and minus tell you what was added, changed and removed. And uv tree shows you where a shared package is needed twice.

points.text: uv add writes a floor, never a pin
uv tree shows who asked for what
